title: The Gospel of John Timeline
sub: Signs and 'I Am' · John's Own Architecture · Every Chapter, Chapter & Verse
desc: The most theologically distinct Gospel, built on seven numbered ‘signs’ and seven ‘I am’ declarations rather than a simple chronology: no parables, no exorcisms, and roughly half the book set across a single final week. Written last of the four, explicitly stating its own purpose at 20:31: so that you may believe.

eras.label: Era One · John 1:1-18
eras.name: Prologue — The Word Made Flesh
eras.dates: No manger, no genealogy: John opens before creation itself

events.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
events.detail: John's opening line deliberately echoes Genesis 1:1 word for word in Greek, 'In the beginning', but pushes the story back before creation itself. The Word (Logos) is both with God and is God, a claim no other Gospel opens with.

events.title: The Word Became Flesh
events.detail: John the Baptist gets a supporting role here, 'not the Light, but a witness to the Light,' before the famous turn: 'the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.' Verse 18 closes the prologue with a claim unique to John: no one has ever seen God, but Jesus 'has explained Him,' the same Greek root that gives us 'exegesis.'

eras.label: Era Two · John 1:19-51
eras.name: Gathering the First Disciples
eras.dates: A chain of one-day scenes: 'the next day... the next day...'

events.title: John's Testimony: 'I Am Not the Christ'
events.detail: Priests and Levites interrogate John the Baptist directly (not the Christ, not Elijah, not 'the Prophet') until he identifies himself only as Isaiah's 'voice crying in the wilderness,' refusing every title they offer him.

events.title: Behold the Lamb of God
events.detail: John names Jesus with the title that will frame the whole Gospel, 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world', timed, deliberately or not, to land right before Passover season, when lambs were the whole point.

events.title: The First Disciples: Andrew, Peter, Philip, Nathanael
events.detail: A chain reaction in one afternoon: Andrew follows Jesus on John's word alone, fetches his brother Simon (renamed Cephas/Peter on sight), and by evening Philip has found Nathanael under a fig tree: the same fig tree Jesus somehow already saw him under before they'd met.

eras.label: Era Three · John 2:1-4:54
eras.name: Two Signs and a Turning Point
eras.dates: Cana to Jerusalem to Samaria to Galilee: the first ‘signs’ begin

events.title: Water into Wine at Cana
events.detail: John's own word for this is 'sign' (sēmeion), not just miracle: the first of seven that structure the whole first half of the book. Six stone jars meant for ceremonial washing get filled with the best wine of the night, and John notes plainly: 'His disciples believed in Him.'

events.title: Cleansing the Temple; 'Destroy This Sanctuary'
events.detail: John places the temple cleansing at the very start of Jesus' ministry, not the last week, as the Synoptics do: a real structural difference scholars still debate. Jesus answers the demand for a sign with a riddle no one understands until after the resurrection: 'destroy this sanctuary, and in three days I will raise it up.'

events.title: Nicodemus by Night; Born Again
events.detail: A Pharisee and member of the ruling council comes secretly, after dark, and gets the most quoted verse in the whole Bible in response: 'For God so loved the world...' The image of being 'born again' plays on a genuine Greek double meaning (anothen: 'again' or 'from above') that trips Nicodemus up on purpose.

events.title: John the Baptist: 'He Must Increase'
events.detail: John's own disciples get jealous on his behalf when Jesus starts baptizing more people than he does. His answer is the last we hear from him in this Gospel: 'He must increase, but I must decrease': the friend of the bridegroom stepping back once the bridegroom has arrived.

events.title: The Woman at the Well
events.detail: A Samaritan woman, alone at a well at noon, itself a detail signaling social isolation, gets the longest recorded one-on-one conversation Jesus has with anyone in any Gospel, and the first person in John he tells outright, 'I who speak to you am He.' Her whole town comes out to see him afterward.

events.title: Healing the Royal Official's Son
events.detail: The second numbered sign, explicitly bookended with the first: John notes this happened 'when He had come out of Judea into Galilee' the same way the Cana miracle did. A father takes Jesus at his word from a distance, 'Go; your son lives', and the healing lines up to the exact hour.

eras.label: Era Four · John 5:1-6:71
eras.name: Sabbath Controversy and Bread from Heaven
eras.dates: Bethesda to the far shore of Galilee: the crowds grow, then thin out

events.title: Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
events.detail: A man who has been sick thirty-eight years gets healed on the Sabbath without even asking Jesus' name first: Jesus finds him again afterward in the temple, the one detail that turns a healing into a Sabbath controversy.

events.title: 'My Father Is Working'; the Son's Authority
events.detail: John states the stakes plainly: the Jewish leaders sought all the more to kill him 'because He not only was breaking the Sabbath, but also was calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.' Jesus doesn't walk the claim back: he doubles down, citing John the Baptist, his own works, and Moses' own writings as three independent witnesses.

events.title: Feeding the Five Thousand
events.detail: The only miracle recorded in all four Gospels: five barley loaves and two fish from a boy in the crowd, twelve baskets left over. John alone records the crowd's response: they try to make Jesus king by force, and he withdraws alone up the mountain to escape it.

events.title: Walking on the Water
events.detail: Rowing against a strong wind in the dark, the disciples see Jesus approaching on the sea and are terrified until his words, 'It is I; do not be afraid', which in the Greek carry the same egō eimi, 'I am,' that echoes God's own name at the burning bush.

events.title: 'I Am the Bread of Life'
events.detail: The crowd that ate the loaves tracks Jesus down the next day still thinking about free bread; he answers with the first of his great 'I am' statements and pushes the image to a genuinely shocking place ('unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood, you have no life in yourselves') language his own listeners call 'a difficult statement.'

events.title: Many Disciples Leave; Peter's Confession
events.detail: The bread of life teaching costs Jesus a large chunk of his following: 'many of His disciples went away and were not walking with Him anymore.' Asked if the Twelve will leave too, Peter's answer becomes one of the Gospel's most quoted lines: 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have words of eternal life.'

eras.label: Era Five · John 7:1-8:59
eras.name: Feast of Booths — Living Water and Light
eras.dates: Jerusalem in the fall, and open division in the crowd

events.title: Jesus Goes Up to the Feast in Secret
events.detail: Even his own brothers don't believe in him yet, and needle him to go public in Jerusalem; he goes anyway, but quietly, arriving only once the feast is already underway, while the crowd argues in whispers about whether he's a good man or a deceiver.

events.title: Teaching in the Temple; Division in the Crowd
events.detail: Jesus teaches openly in the temple despite officers sent to arrest him, and the crowd fractures over him in real time: some call him the Prophet, some the Christ, others object that the Christ can't come from Galilee. Even the temple officers come back empty-handed, telling the chief priests, 'never has a man spoken like this.'

events.title: The Woman Caught in Adultery
events.detail: Scribes and Pharisees stage a legal trap, bring the woman, cite Moses' law, wait for Jesus to either contradict Moses or contradict his own mercy. He does neither, writing silently on the ground until the accusers leave one by one, oldest first: 'let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone.' The oldest and best manuscripts of John don't contain this passage at all: most modern Bibles print it bracketed, as this app's underlying text also marks it, an honest textual note rather than a hidden one.

events.title: 'I Am the Light of the World'
events.detail: Another great 'I am' statement, this one drawing on the huge lampstands lit during the Feast of Booths just behind him. The argument spirals into an extended standoff over Jesus' identity and his Father, ending with a line that will detonate a chapter later: 'unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins.'

events.title: 'Before Abraham Was, I Am'
events.detail: A conversation about freedom and slavery to sin escalates into the sharpest confrontation in the Gospel (Jesus tells a crowd claiming Abraham as their father that they belong to 'the devil,' and closes with the most direct divine-name claim in the whole book: 'before Abraham was, I am') unmistakably Exodus 3:14's language. They pick up stones on the spot.

eras.label: Era Six · John 9:1-10:42
eras.name: Sight, Blindness, and the Good Shepherd
eras.dates: A man born blind becomes the Gospel's own parable about seeing

events.title: Healing the Man Born Blind
events.detail: Asked whose sin caused the blindness, Jesus rejects the premise outright, 'so that the works of God might be manifested in him', then heals with mud and spit and sends the man to wash in the pool of Siloam, whose name John bothers to translate: 'Sent.'

events.title: Interrogated and Cast Out; 'I Do See'
events.detail: The healed man gets interrogated twice by the Pharisees, his own parents distance themselves out of fear, and he's finally thrown out of the synagogue for refusing to recant: at which point Jesus finds him again and he becomes the first person in this Gospel to explicitly worship Jesus. Jesus closes the whole episode on a deliberate irony: 'those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.'

events.title: 'I Am the Good Shepherd'
events.detail: Directly continuing the blind man's story (no scene break in the Greek), Jesus draws out the image of a shepherd who knows his sheep by name against hired hands who flee at the first sign of danger, and states his mission in the starkest terms yet: 'I lay down My life for the sheep... I lay it down. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again.'

events.title: 'I and the Father Are One'
events.detail: Months later, at the winter Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), the same demand returns ('if You are the Christ, tell us openly') and Jesus' answer, 'I and the Father are one,' draws a second stoning attempt. He escapes across the Jordan, to the same place John the Baptist first baptized, and many there believe.

eras.label: Era Seven · John 11:1-12:50
eras.name: Lazarus — the Climactic Sign
eras.dates: The seventh and greatest sign, and the decision that follows it

events.title: 'Lazarus Has Fallen Asleep'
events.detail: Word comes that a close friend is dying, and Jesus deliberately waits two more days before setting out ('this sickness is not to end in death, but is for the glory of God.' Thomas's grim aside to the other disciples) 'let us also go, so that we may die with Him': is the first hint of how dangerous this trip back to Judea really is.

events.title: 'I Am the Resurrection and the Life'; Jesus Wept
events.detail: Martha meets Jesus outside the village with equal parts grief and faith; his answer to her, 'I am the resurrection and the life', is the fifth of the Gospel's great 'I am' statements. Then, confronted with Mary's tears and the mourning crowd, comes the Bible's shortest verse and one of its most human: 'Jesus wept.'

events.title: 'Lazarus, Come Forth'
events.detail: Four days dead, still bound in grave wrappings, Lazarus walks out of the tomb at a single spoken command: the seventh and most dramatic of John's numbered signs, the one that finally forces the religious authorities' hand.

events.title: The Plot to Kill Jesus
events.detail: Caiaphas the high priest argues, without meaning it as prophecy, that it's expedient for one man to die for the nation: John reads this as an unintentional true prophecy about the cross. From this point the council formally moves to have Jesus killed, and he withdraws from public view.

events.title: Anointing at Bethany
events.detail: Six days before Passover, Mary anoints Jesus' feet with nard worth a year's wages and wipes them with her hair; Judas Iscariot's objection is the moment John flags him outright as a thief who used to skim the money box, not merely a future betrayer.

events.title: Triumphal Entry; 'Unless a Grain of Wheat'
events.detail: Palm branches and Hosannas greet Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey's colt, fulfilling Zechariah; Greek pilgrims asking to see him prompt Jesus' own verdict that 'the hour has come.' He answers with an image of a buried seed producing life through death, and a voice from heaven confirms it publicly: the last public words Jesus speaks in this Gospel before withdrawing to his own disciples alone.

eras.label: Era Eight · John 13:1-17:26
eras.name: The Upper Room — Farewell Discourse
eras.dates: The night before the cross, entirely indoors, entirely among friends

events.title: Washing the Disciples' Feet
events.detail: Jesus takes on the lowest servant's task in the room himself, over Peter's objection ('you will never wash my feet, ever!') turning basin-and-towel into an enacted command: 'I gave you an example, that you also should do as I did to you.'

events.title: The Betrayer Named; a New Commandment; Peter's Denial Foretold
events.detail: Jesus identifies his betrayer only obliquely, by dipping bread and handing it to Judas, who leaves immediately into the night. What follows is the Gospel's own summary command ('love one another, even as I have loved you') undercut within verses by Jesus predicting, precisely, that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows.

events.title: 'I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life'
events.detail: Answering Thomas's honest confusion ('we do not know where You are going, how do we know the way?') Jesus gives the most quoted of all his 'I am' statements: 'No one comes to the Father but through Me.'

events.title: The Promise of the Advocate
events.detail: Jesus promises a Helper who will remain after he's gone, 'the Spirit of truth,' and offers a peace explicitly different from anything the world gives: 'not as the world gives do I give to you.' The section closes with Jesus, mid-speech, telling them to get up and leave the room ('get up, let us go from here') though the discourse itself keeps going for three more chapters, a real seam in the text scholars still discuss.

events.title: 'I Am the True Vine'
events.detail: The last of the seven 'I am' sayings: Jesus as the vine, his Father as the vine-grower, the disciples as branches that can do nothing apart from him. The chapter closes on the same command repeated from chapter 13: 'love one another.'

events.title: The World's Hatred; the Spirit's Work
events.detail: Jesus warns bluntly that the same world that hated him will hate his followers, then reframes his own departure as something that actually benefits them, 'it is to your advantage that I go away', because only then does the Advocate come, to convict the world and guide the disciples 'into all the truth.'

events.title: Sorrow Turned to Joy
events.detail: The disciples openly admit they don't understand his riddling talk of 'a little while'; Jesus answers with the image of a woman in labor, pain giving way to a joy no one can take back, and closes the entire discourse on a line of quiet confidence: 'take courage; I have overcome the world.'

events.title: The High Priestly Prayer
events.detail: Jesus stops speaking to the disciples and prays aloud in front of them instead: for his own glorification, for the Eleven by name and role, and finally for 'those also who believe in Me through their word,' meaning every reader of this Gospel by extension. The prayer's central request is unity: 'that they may all be one, even as You, Father, are in Me and I in You.'

eras.label: Era Nine · John 18:1-19:42
eras.name: Betrayal, Trial, and Crucifixion
eras.dates: From a garden across the Kidron to a garden tomb nearby

events.title: Gethsemane; 'I Am He'
events.detail: Judas leads an armed cohort to a garden Jesus often used, and when Jesus identifies himself with the same egō eimi used throughout this Gospel, the whole arresting party falls backward to the ground: a detail found in no other Gospel. Peter draws a sword and is told plainly to put it away: 'the cup which the Father has given Me, shall I not drink it?'

events.title: Before Annas; Peter's Denial
events.detail: Jesus is questioned first by Annas, the power behind the sitting high priest Caiaphas, and answers a question about his teaching by pointing to its total openness: 'I always taught in synagogues and in the temple... I spoke nothing in secret.' Outside, in the courtyard, Peter denies him three times exactly as predicted, ending on the rooster's crow.

events.title: Before Pilate; 'What Is Truth?'
events.detail: The Jewish leaders won't enter Pilate's headquarters themselves, for fear of ritual defilement before Passover, forcing Pilate to shuttle back and forth between them and Jesus. His question to Jesus, 'what is truth?', gets no direct answer, and the crowd chooses to release the insurrectionist Barabbas instead.

events.title: 'Behold the Man'; 'We Have No King but Caesar'
events.detail: Flogged, crowned with thorns, mocked as king in purple, Jesus is presented to the crowd with Pilate's own words: 'behold, the man!' The chief priests' final line to get the execution they want is the Gospel's bleakest irony: a Jewish crowd, under Rome's boot, declaring 'we have no king but Caesar.'

events.title: The Crucifixion
events.detail: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha; Pilate's trilingual sign (Hebrew, Latin, Greek) reading 'JESUS THE NAZARENE, THE KING OF THE JEWS' becomes its own small standoff when the chief priests object and Pilate refuses to change it: 'what I have written I have written.' From the cross Jesus formally entrusts his mother to the disciple he loved.

events.title: 'It Is Finished'
events.detail: Jesus states his thirst to fulfill Scripture, receives sour wine on a hyssop branch, the same plant used to paint lamb's blood on doorposts at the first Passover, and dies with a single declared word, tetelestai, 'it is finished,' a commercial term for a debt fully paid. A soldier's spear thrust afterward, and the blood and water that follow, become their own independent witness in the text.

events.title: Burial in the Garden Tomb
events.detail: Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, and Nicodemus, the same man who first came to Jesus by night in chapter 3, together give Jesus an unusually lavish burial, a hundred litras of myrrh and aloes, in a new tomb in a nearby garden.

eras.label: Era Ten · John 20:1-21:25
eras.name: Resurrection and Epilogue
eras.dates: An empty tomb, a stunned Thomas, and a very ordinary breakfast

events.title: The Empty Tomb
events.detail: Mary Magdalene finds the stone already moved and runs to fetch Peter and 'the disciple whom Jesus loved'; the beloved disciple outruns Peter to the tomb but waits for him to enter first, and it's the careful detail of the neatly folded face-cloth, separate from the wrappings, that convinces him: 'he saw and believed.'

events.title: Mary Magdalene Meets the Risen Jesus
events.detail: Mistaking him for the gardener, Mary only recognizes Jesus when he says her name, 'Mary!', becoming, in this Gospel, the very first witness of the resurrection and the one Jesus sends to tell the others.

events.title: 'Peace Be With You'; the Spirit Given
events.detail: Jesus appears inside a locked room, shows the disciples his wounded hands and side, and breathes on them with a phrase that deliberately echoes God breathing life into Adam in Genesis 2: 'receive the Holy Spirit.'

events.title: Doubting Thomas; the Book's Purpose Stated
events.detail: Absent the first time, Thomas refuses to believe without physical proof; a week later Jesus offers exactly that proof, and Thomas responds with the highest confession in the whole Gospel: 'My Lord and my God!' John then states outright, uniquely among the Gospels, why he wrote the book at all: 'so that you may believe... and that believing you may have life in His name.'

events.title: Breakfast by the Sea; 153 Fish
events.detail: An epilogue most scholars read as added after 20:31 already reads like an ending: seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing until a stranger on the shore redirects the net, and John recognizes him first: 'it is the Lord.' The oddly specific catch, 153 large fish, has invited centuries of symbolic guesswork with no settled answer.

events.title: 'Do You Love Me?'; Peter Restored
events.detail: Three questions answer three denials: 'Simon, son of John, do you love Me?' asked three times over a charcoal fire, the same detail as the fire where Peter denied him, each answer converted into a commission to 'feed my sheep.' The Gospel closes admitting its own limits: 'many other things Jesus did... the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.'
